To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

a noninvertible 12-parameter, second-order polynomial image transformation model, a hierarchical, robust estimation technique, and an algorithm for constructing image registration graphs, together enable the mosaicing of multiple images onto a mosaic anchor image with a high degree of accuracy and coverage.

a noniterative, linear, feature-based method for jointly estimating image-to-mosaic transformations can be constructed by combining constraints derived from pairwise registration with an incremental graph-based technique for constructing the set of registered pairs.

a noninvertible 12-parameter, second-degree polynomial image transformation model, a hierarchical, robust estimation technique for registering pairs of uncalibrated retinal images, and a feature-based, non-iterative linear technique for estimating the consistent transformations of all retinal images to the mosaic anchor image, can be combined to produce a mosaic that is more accurate than previously published methods and covers a broader area of the retina.

the development of techniques for the construction of image mosaics, or "mosaic atlases," of the human retina, which are needed for the development of automated, computer-based, diagnostic systems.
the development of a technique for constructing image mosasics from multiple, weak-perspective retinal images.
the construction of mosaics of retinal images from multiple, unregistered views.

The main takeaway from our work is that
it is possible to construct mosaics from a set of retinal images that do not all overlap.

the problem of mosaicing images with a high-order image-to-mosaic transformation can be solved using a simple linear estimation technique that exploits the fact that pairwise image-to-mosaic transformations are linear.

a simple linear estimation technique can produce a high-quality mosaic of the retina, even when there are significant differences in the retinal geometry and the images are acquired from different viewing positions.
